big_idea: Motivation is not a prerequisite for success but a byproduct of it. Haden argues high achievers don't wait to feel inspired, they start despite the absence of motivation, and small visible wins generate the momentum that keeps them going.

tool.label: Process goals, not outcome goals
tool.text: Instead of fixating on a distant outcome, set a goal once and then largely forget it, concentrating daily effort on a specific, repeatable process so consistent small wins build the momentum that outcome-focus can't.
tool.note: Haden frames this as what separates people who look motivated from people who actually finish things: the process, not the initial spark of inspiration, is what's sustainable.

ideas.title: Motivation follows action
ideas.text: Preparation and starting, even reluctantly, build enough early confidence to cross the first hurdle; motivation shows up afterward, not before.

ideas.title: The reward-loop effect
ideas.text: Every small, visible win triggers the brain's reward center, creating a positive feedback loop that pulls you toward the next step without relying on willpower.

ideas.title: Serial achievement over single-minded specialization
ideas.text: Haden argues most successful people build competence in a domain over roughly 5 to 7 years, then move on to a new challenge.

ideas.title: Decision minimization
ideas.text: Turn recurring choices into fixed routines to save willpower for the moments that matter.

ideas.title: Work your number
ideas.text: Treat success as probabilistic; increase your rate of attempts rather than trying to perfect your strategy in advance.

ideas.title: Share routines, not goals
ideas.text: Talking about your goal too early triggers a satisfaction response that can undercut follow-through; talk about your daily process instead.

try_it: Pick one goal you've stalled on and rewrite it as a daily process rather than an outcome, tracking only the process this week.
Start one task today specifically without waiting to feel motivated; notice whether momentum shows up afterward.
Identify one recurring decision and turn it into a fixed, automatic routine to remove that daily choice.
Instead of announcing your big goal to friends, tell one person your process instead and ask them to check in.
best_for: Entrepreneurs and people in early-stage grinds, startups, fitness goals, creative projects
Chronic goal-abandoners who keep waiting to feel ready
less_useful: Readers wanting research-heavy, citation-driven arguments, since Haden leans on anecdotes and his own journalism experience
People whose motivation struggles stem from clinical factors like depression or ADHD, which the book doesn't really address

related.why: A faster trigger for the same start-before-you-feel-ready principle
The systems-and-cues mechanics behind turning a process into a lasting habit
